73c40ff0e1:
The guide gives 7.3 one phrase, preventing destructive actions, and 7.4 a title, identity, secrets and keys. This chapter treats them together, because they answer the same question from two sides: what stops an agent from doing damage when the model gets something wrong, or is steered by an attacker?

Hooks are the deterministic gate on actions. Identity and secret handling decide how much damage any action can do, and whether a credential can be stolen through the context window.

On the hooks side we cover:

  • hooks as enforcement rather than advice;
  • the Claude Code and Agent SDK hook events that matter for safety;
  • a PreToolUse guard traced end to end;
  • the hook contract (input JSON, exit codes, output fields);
  • ordering with permission rules;
  • the three ways hooks fail (slow, crashing, bypassed).

On the identity side: API key types, workspaces, rotation, where keys must never be, secrets inside agent environments, keeping secrets out of context and transcripts, OAuth for MCP servers, and short-lived credentials.
18b6f02526:
Reading time: about 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 20 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/20-hooks-secrets/ (run bash run_all.sh; all offline).

The centrepiece is guard.py, a working PreToolUse command hook, with 31 sample hook inputs in samples/. secrets_lib.py is the shared secret detector. The scanner, the redaction hooks and the transcript redactor all use it.
76546d2c3d: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 02 introduced hooks as the place for deterministic actions (events, HookMatcher, formatter and Stop-gate examples), and this chapter doesn't repeat that. Chapter 10 owns settings files, scopes and precedence. Chapter 19 owns prompt injection, least privilege, guardrail layering and PII, the threats these controls answer. Chapter 21 covers tool design and approval patterns. Chapter 22 covers MCP servers, including the server side of OAuth.
5d28443cd9:
Together the two objectives are 2.6% of the exam, so expect one or two direct items. The ideas also turn up inside scenario questions in other domains. "The agent ran a destructive command" and "the key leaked" are the two failure stories any agent design question can end with.

Wrong options follow a pattern:

  • They put a guarantee in a prompt ("tell the agent never to run rm -rf").
  • They trust a filter that matches strings.
  • They give the model a credential and ask it to be careful.
  • They use one long-lived shared key for everything.

The right option moves the rule into code at a lifecycle point. Or it moves the credential out of the model's reach. Or it shrinks what the credential can do.
b9bdc4a3aa: Nothing in this chapter is new to security engineering. What's new is the thing being controlled: a component that chooses its own actions, reads attacker-controlled text as part of its input, and can be talked into things. The old ideas still apply. Knowing where they come from helps you see why the exam's right answers look the way they do.
10248ff497:
The reference monitor (1972). James Anderson's report for the US Air Force defined a reference monitor as a mechanism with three properties. It mediates every access by a subject to an object. It's tamper-proof. And it's small enough to be verified. Each property maps onto hook design:

  • Always invoked: the hook must sit on every path to the tool. That's why bypasses through other tools matter (section 10).
  • Tamper-proof: the agent must not be able to edit the hook or its settings. That's why guard.py protects .claude/settings.json and .claude/hooks/.
  • Verifiable: the hook must be small and tested. That's why section 13 treats it like any other security control, with a regression suite.
95781c3004: Least privilege and fail-safe defaults (1975). Saltzer and Schroeder's design principles say two things here. Every program should run with the least privilege it needs. And access decisions should default to denial when something is unclear. The first is the basis of workspace-scoped keys and per-workload service accounts. The second is the basis of fail-closed hooks: a guard that crashes must block, not allow.
cc42da7f12:
Interceptors. Version-control hooks (pre-commit, pre-receive), servlet filters, Spring's HandlerInterceptor and AOP @Around advice are all the same pattern: code that runs at a defined point whether or not the business logic remembers it.

Git's pre-receive hook is the closest relative of a PreToolUse deny. It runs on the server and can reject a push whatever the client was configured to do. That's why shared repositories enforce "no force-push to main" there, and not in a developer's local config.
19bb696811:
The confused deputy (1988). Norm Hardy described a compiler with write access to a billing file. A user tricked it into overwriting that file by naming it as the output. The program used its own authority for a request that came from someone else.

An agent holding a broad service credential while reading a customer's email is the same deputy. The modern fix is to propagate the requester's identity (capability-style tokens, OAuth on-behalf-of), so the downstream system can say no.
a32467462b:
Secrets management. The history moves in steps:

  • Twelve-factor apps (2011) moved configuration, including credentials, out of code and into the environment.
  • HashiCorp Vault (2015) and the cloud secret managers then took them out of plain environment variables, and added leasing, rotation and audit.
  • OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, 2012) separated the user who grants access from the client that uses it. The OAuth 2.0 token-exchange spec (RFC 8693, 2020) defined how one service trades a token for another.
  • Workload identity (SPIFFE, 2017; cloud OIDC federation from about 2019; GitHub Actions OIDC, 2021) removed the last long-lived secret from many pipelines. The platform vouches for the workload, and the workload exchanges that proof for a short-lived token.

The Claude API supports the same pattern as Workload Identity Federation.
054bf28baf: Agent harnesses. Claude Code shipped hooks in mid-2025. It started with a handful of events, and shell commands that read JSON on stdin. The Agent SDK exposes the same events as in-process callbacks. By late 2026 the hooks reference lists more than thirty events and several handler types: command, HTTP, MCP tool, prompt, and an experimental agent type. The core contract hasn't changed. JSON in, a decision out, exit code 2 to block.
62f4db6496: Suppose the requirement is "the agent must never force-push to main". In a Claude Code or Agent SDK deployment there are four places you can put that rule. They differ in one property that matters more than any other: does the rule depend on the model choosing to follow it?
89eff219a0:
1. The prompt (system prompt, CLAUDE.md, a skill). The model reads the rule and usually follows it. "Usually" is the problem.

The rule competes with everything else in the context. It can be diluted in a long session, lost in compaction, or argued away by text that looks authoritative, which is exactly what an indirect prompt injection is (chapter 19). The model may also reach the same effect by a route the rule-writer didn't foresee: git push origin +main is a force push with no --force in it. A prompt rule has a non-zero failure rate that you can't measure in advance and can't drive to zero.

Prompts still matter. They shape what the agent tries to do, so a good prompt reduces how often the hard controls have to fire. They aren't enforcement.
eeec036b01:
2. Permission rules (permissions.allow, ask, deny in settings; allowed_tools and disallowed_tools in the SDK). The harness evaluates these, not the model, so they're deterministic. They're pattern matches on the tool name and a simple form of its argument: Bash(git push --force *), Read(./.env), WebFetch(domain:example.com). Evaluation goes deny first, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins.

The permissions docs warn that Bash rules which try to constrain arguments are fragile. Bash(curl *) doesn't match /usr/bin/curl or sh -c 'curl ...'. Permission rules are the right tool for coarse decisions, such as "this agent has no WebFetch" or "never read .env". They're the wrong tool for semantic ones like "no destructive git operations".
3faa9e4c0b:
3. Hooks. Your code runs at a lifecycle point and receives the full structured tool input. It can parse a shell command, resolve a path, look up a ticket, check the time of day or call a policy service. Then it can allow, deny, ask, defer or rewrite.

Hooks are as deterministic as your code and as expressive as a general-purpose language. That's the reason 7.3 exists as an objective. They also have failure modes of their own (section 10), and they only see what passes through the tool interface.
29b22b92d0:
4. The environment (sandbox, container, network proxy, credentials scope). The operating system or the network enforces the rule, below the agent and below the hooks. Say the container's git credential can't push to main because branch protection on the server forbids it. Then no sequence of tool calls can do it.

This is the strongest layer, and the coarsest. It can't tell "delete the build directory" from "delete the source directory" when both are writable. Section 18 covers the agent-environment side.
3ccf278d42:
For a must-never requirement, the exam answer is almost always "a deterministic control": a hook, a permission rule or an environment restriction, and usually a combination. A useful rule of thumb:

  • the coarse rule goes in permissions;
  • the semantic rule goes in a hook;
  • the last line of defence goes in the environment;
  • the explanation goes in the prompt, so the agent rarely needs stopping.
8a821a61bc:
Chapter 02 walked through the hook lifecycle for deterministic actions such as formatting, audit logging and test gates. For safety, a smaller set of events carries most of the weight. The property that matters for each is whether it can prevent something or only observe it.

The Claude Code hooks reference (checked October 2026) lists 33 events. The table covers the ones with a safety role, and whether the Agent SDK supports them as in-process callbacks. The Python SDK supports fewer events than TypeScript. Anything the Python SDK lacks can still run as a shell hook from settings files, provided setting_sources loads them.
a9c8b1294d:
Three facts in the table are worth memorising.

First, only "pre" events prevent. PostToolUse fires after rm has already deleted the files. It can hide the output, warn, or stop the agent from continuing, but the action has happened. A question that asks how to prevent something and offers PostToolUse is offering the wrong event.

Second, PreToolUse runs before the permission rules are applied, for every tool call. That's what makes it the right place for a check that must see every call. Compare the SDK's can_use_tool callback, which chapter 02 showed only sees calls that would otherwise prompt.

Third, matchers see only the tool name, never the arguments. A matcher of Bash sends every shell command to your hook, and the hook decides by reading tool_input.
60d953fc34: A command hook is a program. For each matching event, Claude Code starts it, writes one JSON object to its stdin, and waits for it to exit (up to a timeout). Then it reads the exit code, stdout and stderr. Everything about hook design follows from that contract, so it's worth knowing exactly.
9e61ed8f97:
Input. Every event carries the common fields session_id, transcript_path, cwd, permission_mode and hook_event_name. There are a few newer ones too, such as prompt_id and effort, plus agent_id/agent_type inside subagents. PreToolUse adds tool_name, tool_input (the exact arguments the model produced) and tool_use_id.

Two of these deserve care. transcript_path points to the full session transcript on disk. A hook can read context from it, and anyone who can read that file can read every secret that ever entered the session (section 19). cwd is where the session is, not necessarily the project root. Use $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR to locate your own scripts and to anchor path checks.
fe46f737ee: Exit 0: success. If stdout is a single JSON object, it's parsed for decisions. Otherwise it's plain text, which on a few events (UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart) is added as context for Claude. Claude never sees stderr from an exit-0 hook.
05cd17a186: Exit 2: a blocking error on events that can block. stderr is the reason, and it's fed back to Claude. Exit 2 blocks even when stdout contains JSON that says allow. Per the permissions docs, a hook that exits 2 stops the call before permission rules are evaluated, so the block beats any allow rule.
6427fef3d8: The third rule is the one people get wrong. A Python guard that raises KeyError exits with code 1, and the destructive command runs. Section 10 comes back to this. There are two fixes. Make the guard fail closed itself (catch everything, exit 2). Or configure the hook with onFailure: "block", which the reference says makes a failure behave like exit 2 on that event.
37f5d81527:
Output fields. On exit 0, the JSON can carry universal fields and event-specific ones. The universal ones are:

  • continue (default true); false stops Claude entirely and takes precedence over any event decision;
  • stopReason, shown to the user when continue is false;
  • systemMessage, a warning shown to the user, not the model;
  • suppressOutput, still accepted but documented as having no effect.

For PreToolUse the decision lives in hookSpecificOutput, which must name its hookEventName:
923c6bdc81:
Other events use a top-level decision: "block" with a reason (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop, ConfigChange, PreCompact).

Older material shows PreToolUse hooks returning a top-level decision: "approve"/"block". Current docs use hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision for PreToolUse. Prefer that form, and read the older one as legacy.
478f5f91e0:
Hook types other than command follow the same JSON contract over a different transport:

  • An http hook POSTs the input and reads the response body.
  • An mcp_tool hook calls a tool on a configured MCP server.
  • A prompt hook asks a model for a single-turn JSON verdict.
  • The experimental agent hook runs a subagent with read-only tools.

For a destructive-action guard, prefer command or http. A prompt hook puts a model back in the decision path, and that brings back the probabilistic failure you were trying to remove. It can be a useful extra layer, a second opinion on ambiguous commands you'd otherwise ask about. It shouldn't be the only gate.

Default timeouts are 600 seconds for command, HTTP and MCP-tool hooks (30 seconds on UserPromptSubmit and the model-switch events), 30 seconds for prompt hooks and 60 for agent hooks. A guard should set its own short timeout. Section 10 explains why.
649d4de955: Here's one blocked call from start to finish, using the companion's guard.py. A developer asks Claude Code to "clean up the broken canary release". Somewhere in a long session, the model decides the quickest clean-up is to delete the namespace. Nothing in the prompt forbids it in so many words. And even if something did, the session is 40 turns long.
f108a7c8a3: The model emits a tool call. The assistant message ends with a tool_use block, {"name": "Bash", "input": {"command": "kubectl delete ns billing-canary"}}, and stop_reason is "tool_use".
90fcda7de0: The guard parses the command. shlex splits it into one simple command, ["kubectl", "delete", "ns", "billing-canary"]. There are no wrappers to strip and no nested shell. The program is kubectl and the verb is delete.
afb8bccf89: The model receives the reason as the result of its tool call, marked as an error. It reads "use kubectl get/describe and propose the change". So it runs a read-only command and reports back instead of deleting.
21006891b3:
Step 7 is what separates a good guard from a merely correct one. A denial with no reason, or with just "blocked", leaves the model to guess. It often retries the same thing with different syntax, which is exactly the probing you don't want. A reason that names the safe alternative turns the block into guidance.

Companion example 17 runs the whole loop with two hooks registered: the guard, and a careless "approve everything" hook. Deny wins, the reason reaches the model, and the only command that ever executes is the read-only one:
f7114b6ed1: Run 01_guard_on_samples.py to see the same decision for all 31 sample inputs. Each sample is a real-shaped PreToolUse payload, piped to the guard exactly as Claude Code would pipe it:
908e2752e6:
Note the three outcomes:

  • Most calls get no opinion ({} or empty stdout). The normal permission flow decides, and the guard grants nothing.
  • Clearly destructive calls get deny.
  • Calls that might be fine but can't be judged statically get ask: rm -rf build/ inside the project, a command substitution, a kubectl call against a production namespace.

In a headless CI run, nobody is there to answer an ask, so decide what it means in that context. Usually it becomes a deny, through a PermissionRequest hook, the permission mode, or a stricter guard configuration for CI.
33495550ee: The obvious first guard is a regular expression over the command string. It fails in both directions at once. It misses destructive commands written in any form the author didn't think of. And it blocks harmless commands that merely mention the words. Example 02 runs a naive pattern and the parser-based guard over the same corpus:
bbd117a3a5: The parser-based guard works the way a shell does, in stages. So its view of the command matches what will actually run. That's the property a reference monitor needs.
a7094609fa: Refuse what cannot be analysed statically. Command substitution ($(...), backticks), process substitution, eval, source, and base64 -d in a pipeline all produce the real command only at run time. The guard can't know what they'll do, so it answers ask.
e9278714e9: Resolve paths before matching. For rm targets and for Write/Edit/Read paths, expand ~, join with cwd, and resolve with realpath. Then src/../.env and a symlink pointing at .env both resolve to the protected file (example 06).
aaf05eb6a9:
The parser still isn't a proof. Shell is a large language, and a guard will never anticipate every way of reaching a dangerous effect: a Python one-liner that calls shutil.rmtree, a Makefile target, a script the agent writes and then runs.

That's no reason to skip the guard. It's the reason the guard is one layer among several, with the environment (section 18) as the floor. The guard's job is to stop the common and the obvious with zero failure rate, send the uncertain to a human, and make the agent's normal path the safe one.
c5444ecf82:
A guard's rule set is a policy. The same questions apply to it as to any access policy: what's covered, why, and what the agent is told instead. The classes below cover most real incidents with coding and operations agents. For each one, decide whether the answer is:

  • deny: never acceptable from the agent;
  • ask: sometimes legitimate, and a human can tell;
  • rewrite: acceptable in a safer form that the hook can produce with updatedInput.
731081f489:
Two of the rows protect the guard itself.

Self-modification matters because an agent that can edit .claude/settings.json can delete the hook entry. And an agent that can write to .claude/hooks/guard.py can replace the guard with exit 0. A prompt-injected agent will try both, if the payload was written by someone who knows how Claude Code works.

Secret access matters because a key that enters the context window has, in effect, leaked. It's sent to the API on every later turn, written to the transcript on disk, and may be repeated by the model in its own output (section 19).
0096f8e402:
Rewrite instead of refusing when a safe form exists. Chapter 02's pin_prod_namespace hook appended --context prod-readonly to every kubectl call. Other common rewrites:

  • add --dry-run=server to kubectl apply;
  • turn terraform apply into terraform plan;
  • add -i (interactive) to rm in a local session;
  • point a Write into a sandbox directory, which is the docs' own example of updatedInput.

How the rewrite runs depends on the decision paired with it. With permissionDecision: "allow" it runs immediately. With "ask" it shows the rewritten call to the user. If permissionDecision is omitted, the rewritten input goes through the normal permission evaluation.

Always return a new object rather than mutating tool_input. And don't combine a rewrite with defer, which ignores it.
952a732905:
Write reasons for the model, not for a log. "Blocked" teaches nothing. "Force push / remote branch deletion rewrites shared history; push a new branch and open a PR" tells the model what to do next.

An attacker who controls the model's input can see the reason too. So keep internal detail out of it: hostnames, the full rule list, how to get an exception. Name the safe path and stop there.
0818815929: Real deployments have more than one hook and more than one source of rules. Managed settings from the security team, project settings in the repository, a developer's user settings, plugin hooks, and SDK callbacks in your application can all apply to the same tool call. The exam can ask what happens when they disagree. The rules are short.
a54b2336d5: Hooks run in parallel. All matching hooks for an event start together, and completion order isn't deterministic. Never write a hook that depends on another having run first. If two checks depend on each other, put them in one hook. Identical handlers defined in more than one settings file run once; a plugin's copy stays separate.
0bfa079562: Among hooks, the most restrictive decision wins: deny beats defer, which beats ask, which beats allow. One deny blocks the call whatever the others return. That's why the careless "approve everything" hook in example 17 couldn't override the guard.
5eb6e8adc3:
Hooks and permission rules. A PreToolUse hook runs before the permission prompt. A hook allow skips the prompt, but it doesn't bypass permission rules. The permissions docs say deny and ask rules are evaluated regardless of what the hook returned. So a matching deny rule still blocks, and a matching ask rule still prompts.

In the other direction, a hook that exits 2 stops the call before permission rules are evaluated, so it overrides allow rules. The docs suggest exactly this pattern for "allow every Bash command except a few": put "Bash" in the allow list and register a PreToolUse hook that rejects the exceptions.
7d57e2d223:
Across settings scopes, hooks merge. Hook entries from user, project, local, managed and plugin sources are combined, not replaced. Permission rules also combine, with deny evaluated before allow across all scopes. A user-level deny blocks a project-level allow, and the reverse.

Two settings give administrators control over the hooks themselves:

  • disableAllHooks turns hooks off. It can't disable managed hooks unless it's set at the managed level.
  • allowManagedHooksOnly, set in managed settings, blocks user, project, local and plugin hooks, so only the hooks the security team ships can run. Use it when the hooks are a compliance control and you don't want a repository adding hooks of its own.

Chapter 10 covers the full settings precedence.
d4f10f72b3: One newer wrinkle. Claude Code mods (plugins that handle a tool.check) answer after rules and hooks. The permissions docs say a mod can approve a call that a PreToolUse hook blocked, unless that hook is in managed settings. So if an organisation lets developers install mods, a guard that must hold belongs in managed settings. This detail is recent and version-specific; check the docs before you rely on it.
7178c65380:
Every PreToolUse hook sits on the critical path of every matching tool call. Take a guard that takes 400 ms, matched against every tool in a session with 300 tool calls. It adds two minutes of waiting. Developers respond by turning it off or narrowing its matcher, which is a bypass in slow motion.

The default timeout for command hooks is 600 seconds, far too long for a guard. Set timeout explicitly (the companion uses 10 seconds), and keep the guard fast:

  • no network calls on the hot path;
  • a tight matcher (Bash|Write|Edit|Read|^mcp__, not every tool);
  • anything slow (audit shipping, notifications) moved into a separate hook that returns async output, so the agent doesn't wait for it.

The Agent SDK docs show {"async_": True, "asyncTimeout": 30000} in Python. Async hooks can't block or modify anything, which is why they're only for side effects.
9139382190:
What happens when a guard does time out? For the Agent SDK, the hooks guide is explicit, and it has changed across versions:

  • A timed-out PreToolUse callback means the tool call doesn't run. Claude receives a tool result saying the hook didn't respond.
  • A timed-out UserPromptSubmit callback blocks the prompt, because a callback there "can be acting as a policy gate that must not fail open".
  • A timed-out Stop callback counts as no decision.

Command hooks differ. The reference says a timed-out UserPromptSubmit hook's output is discarded, and the prompt goes through without it unless onFailure: "block" is set.

The general lesson: know, for your harness and version, whether a timeout fails open or closed on each event, and configure onFailure: "block" on guards where it must fail closed. Treat the per-event timeout behaviour as "check the docs for your version".
5e986cedba:
A crash is an exit code other than 0 or 2. Section 05 showed that it's a non-blocking error: the action proceeds. Malformed stdout on exit 0 is also a non-blocking error: a debug print before the JSON, two JSON objects, a stack trace.

So the most common guard bug, an unhandled exception on an input shape the author didn't expect, silently turns the guard off. And it does so for exactly the unusual calls you most wanted checked. Example 05 runs five hook bodies with both settings of onFailure:
fd54eab814:
The fix has two parts, and you want both.

Inside the guard, wrap the whole body in a catch-all that writes the error to stderr and exits 2, as guard.py does. Then a bug blocks the call and tells you about it, instead of silently allowing it.

In the configuration, set onFailure: "block". Then failures the guard can't catch also block: the interpreter missing, the file not executable, an out-of-memory kill.

Fail-closed guards have a cost. A broken guard stops all work. That cost is the point, because a broken guard should be loud. Keep the guard's dependencies minimal (standard library only in the companion), so it rarely breaks for environmental reasons.
2acd85a379: Another tool reaches the same effect. The guard checks Bash, but the agent uses Write to create cleanup.sh and then runs bash cleanup.sh. Or it uses a Python one-liner, or an MCP tool with filesystem access. Answer: match every tool that can cause the effect (file tools, MCP tools by ^mcp__), treat "run a script the agent just wrote" as ask, and rely on the environment as the floor.
a54f1725f8: The hook is not loaded. Examples: an SDK application whose setting_sources omits the source holding the shell hooks; a CI job that runs with --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'; a developer who ran with a different config directory. Answer: in SDK apps, register safety hooks as callbacks in code instead of relying on settings files. In Claude Code, ship the guard in managed settings, which project settings can't disable.
26b212609e: A higher-priority path approves the call. Examples: bypass permission mode, a mod approving after a hook block, or an allow rule combined with a hook that only returns ask. Answer: set disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" in managed settings, put guards in managed settings, and use deny rather than ask for the must-never list.
1a8c10e7bb: The hook itself is the attack. Project hooks are shell commands that run on the developer's machine. A malicious repository can ship a .claude/settings.json whose hook exfiltrates ~/.aws/credentials the moment a session starts. Claude Code applies project hooks only after the workspace trust dialog is accepted. The hooks reference notes that before v2.1.218, project subagent frontmatter hooks could run from untrusted folders. Treat "trust this folder" like "run this repository's install script", and review .claude/ in a repository you didn't write before trusting it.
b49eed4830:
"The team added a PreToolUse hook that blocks rm -rf, but last night the agent deleted the data directory." Ask which failure mode explains it. The candidates: a crash on an unusual input (exit 1, fail open), a different tool (a Python script), a disguised command (find . -delete), or a session that didn't load the hook.

The best answer fixes the class of failure: fail closed, cover the other tools, put the floor in the environment. Adding one more regex isn't that answer.
3942eba3dd:
PostToolUse: clean what the model will see. Tools return text that can contain secrets. docker compose config prints resolved environment variables; a failing test prints a DSN with a password; a log contains a bearer token.

A PostToolUse hook can replace the result before Claude sees it, using updatedToolOutput (any tool, both SDKs; the older updatedMCPToolOutput covers MCP tools only). It can also add additionalContext telling the model to refer to secrets by name. It can't undo the command, so pair it with the PreToolUse deny on obvious secret reads. Example 07:
38655bdd8b: The fingerprint (first 8 hex characters of a SHA-256) lets an operator correlate "the same secret appeared in three places" without anyone seeing the value. If the secret space is small enough to brute-force, use a keyed hash (HMAC).
822cf15089:
UserPromptSubmit: stop the user from leaking. The most common way a credential enters a session is a person pasting it: "here's the key, try it". A hook on this event sees the prompt before the model does. It can block it with decision: "block" and a reason, which the user sees, and the prompt isn't sent.

Example 08 blocks a pasted Anthropic key and a DSN with a password, and passes a normal question. Its reason tells the user to treat the key as exposed and rotate it, because it has already left their clipboard.
13ce6dc3b0: Stop: a security gate on completion. The test-gate pattern from chapter 02 works for security checks as well. The agent can't say "done" until a secret scan of the diff (git diff | gitleaks, or the companion scanner) is clean. Respect stop_hook_active, so a failing scan can't trap the agent in an endless loop.
f51edae322: ConfigChange: stop self-loosening. If a settings file changes during a session, this hook can block the change. It can't block managed policy settings, which only administrators change. It's a backstop for the self-modification row in section 08.
5297dab44e: PreCompact and transcripts. Compaction summarises the conversation, and the summary can keep a secret the original contained. A PreCompact hook that archives a redacted copy of the transcript (example 14) gives you an audit trail, without a second copy of every secret.
cfa60a3fb3: If you build your own loop on the Messages API (chapter 02), the guard belongs inside the dispatcher, on the only code path that executes tools. For a Spring reader, that's an interceptor in front of a ToolExecutor, the same shape as a HandlerInterceptor for controllers. The Java version below assumes a ShellParser port of the companion's parsing stages.
d6ff9e53f0: The design point is the same in every form. There must be exactly one path from "the model asked" to "the tool ran", and the guard sits on it. A dispatcher that calls some tools through the guarded executor and others directly has a bypass built in.
8b7922ace9:
In an Agent SDK application, the guard is an async callback registered with HookMatcher. The decision logic is the same function. Only the transport changes: a Python dict in and out, instead of stdin, stdout and exit codes.

For a service, the callback form has three advantages. It can't fail to load because a settings file wasn't read. It shares your service's logging and metrics. And your normal unit tests cover it.
b927deee7f:
Test with recorded inputs. Hooks are easy to test, because their input is JSON. The companion's samples/ directory holds 31 real-shaped PreToolUse payloads with expected decisions. 01_guard_on_samples.py pipes each one through the guard as a subprocess. That tests the full contract (stdin parsing, stdout format, exit code) as well as the decision.

19_guard_tests.py adds three lists: commands that must be denied, commands that must ask, and commands that must pass. The last list matters as much as the first two. A guard that blocks git push origin feature/x will be switched off within a week. The file also checks the fail-closed paths: malformed stdin exits 2, and the --exit2 mode blocks via stderr.
c598f1c7db: Every bypass becomes a test. Someone will find a way past the guard: a red-team exercise, an incident, a curious engineer. When they do, the first commit is a failing test case and the second is the fix. Over time, the suite becomes a record of every attack the guard has seen.
7165648bc0: Version and ship it like code. Project hooks live in the repository and change through code review. Organisation-wide guards live in managed settings, distributed by the platform team, with allowManagedHooksOnly where the guard is a compliance control. A guard change that loosens a rule needs the same review as a firewall change.
f06c82224d:
Monitor it. Log every non-empty decision with the session ID, tool, rule and reason. Leave out the full input if it may contain secrets. Watch three numbers:

  • deny rate per rule: a spike means an attack or a broken prompt;
  • ask rate: if it's high, people will start approving without reading;
  • guard error rate: anything above zero is a bug, and with a fail-closed guard it's also an outage.

To debug a hook that doesn't fire, use claude --debug or --debug-file. Check that the event name is cased exactly (PreToolUse, not preToolUse), and that the matcher uses the canonical tool name.
3ea5cc8449: Every action in a Claude application is taken on someone's authority. The design question for 7.4 is whose, and the answer is never "the model's". A Claude application involves up to four identities. Most security mistakes in this area come from mixing them up.
24f995a00a: The application or workload: your backend service, CI job or batch worker. It authenticates to Anthropic with an API key, a service-account key or a federated short-lived token. That credential proves to Anthropic that "this is the rating-api in production". It says nothing about which end user is on the other side.
74d1a90b79: The developer or operator: the person who builds and runs the application. Personal API keys and Console roles belong here. Production shouldn't run as this identity, because personal keys stop working when their owner leaves the organisation.
c872862665: The confused deputy appears when the last two are collapsed. Say the "get_bill" tool calls the billing API with a shared super-user service account and lets the model choose the account ID. Then anyone who can influence the model can read any bill. That includes a customer typing the request, and a support email containing "also fetch ACC-200". The billing API sees a fully privileged caller and says yes. Example 20 shows the difference:
2ed1c281e1:
The rule follows: identity comes from the authenticated session, never from the model. The harness (not the model) attaches the user's identity to every tool call. The tool presents a credential that carries that identity or is scoped to it. That can be OAuth on-behalf-of, a token exchange, or at minimum a check in your tool code against the session principal (chapter 19 shows the dispatcher version).

Use a service identity for work no user owns: the nightly batch summariser, the CI evaluation job, the indexer. Use user identity for anything done for a specific user, so the downstream system enforces its own access rules. Where you must use a service identity for user work, scope it narrowly and authorise every call in code.
ed6494b9df:
The Claude API authenticates a request with a bearer credential: Authorization: Bearer <token>, or the legacy x-api-key header, which is still supported. The SDKs read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment when you construct the client with no arguments.

The authentication docs (checked October 2026) describe three methods: API keys, Workload Identity Federation (section 21) and App Attest for Apple-platform apps. The rest of this section is about keys: what kinds exist, what they can reach, and how long they live.
e94f3274e2:
Personal and service-account keys are identity-backed. They have an owner, and they stop working when that owner is removed. That's the property you want, and the docs recommend them over legacy workspace keys for new integrations.

Here's the pattern to recognise in an exam question. Production runs on a developer's personal key, and fails the day that developer leaves. The answer is a service account per workload.
af4cfe3060:
Workspaces are the scoping unit. Every request runs in exactly one workspace and can reach only that workspace's resources: Files, Message Batches and Skills, plus prompt caches. On the Claude API those are isolated per workspace; on Bedrock and Vertex AI, per organisation.

Each workspace can have its own spend limit and rate limits (requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute). These are set at or below the organisation's limits, never above them.

Roles are assigned per workspace: Workspace User (playground only), Limited Developer, Developer (create keys, use the API), Admin and Billing. Organisation admins get Workspace Admin everywhere, but ordinary developers must be added to each workspace explicitly.

An organisation has a Default Workspace that can't be archived and can't have limits, and a default cap of 100 workspaces. Archiving a workspace archives every key created for it within seconds, and it can't be undone.
c1aaa4dd4b:
Key scope follows from that. A single-workspace key always runs in its workspace, so requests can omit the workspace header. A multi-workspace key must send anthropic-workspace-id on every request. Without it you get 400 invalid_request_error, and an unknown or inaccessible workspace returns 404.

Responses carry the anthropic-workspace-id header, so you can confirm where a request ran. The docs advise creating single-workspace keys unless you need several workspaces. Example 11 models the resolution rules:
24729651be:
A practical layout for a telecom organisation:

  • One workspace per environment and use case (prod-care-assistant, prod-rating-batch, staging, dev-sandbox). Each gets a spend limit that turns a leaked key or a runaway agent loop into a bounded cost.
  • One service account per workload, added only to its workspace, with a single-workspace key or a federation rule.
  • Developers get personal keys in dev-sandbox, and no production keys at all.

The Admin API lists and retrieves keys. It never returns the secret value, only a partial_key_hint, along with fields such as status, workspace_id, created_by and expires_at. That makes it the basis for a nightly audit: keys with no expiry, keys owned by departed users, keys unused for 30 days.
b5a114ec6b:
Expiration is chosen when the key is created, and can't be changed later. The presets are 3 hours, 1 day, 7 days and 30 days. There's also a custom duration, or "Never", meant for keys you rotate yourself through a secrets manager. An organisation can set a maximum expiry policy, which removes "Never".

The creator gets warning emails 7 days before expiry (for keys living at least 14 days) and 1 day before (for at least 7 days). Shorter-lived keys expire with no warning. An expired key returns 401 and can't be reactivated. Expiry limits how long a leaked key is useful, but the docs say not to rely on it alone.
044a575f67: The outline names three places a key must never be. Each is wrong for a different reason, and the exam may ask for the reason, not just the rule.
f84800c942:
Not in a prompt. Anything in the context window is sent to the API on every turn. It's stored wherever you log requests, written to the session transcript, possibly cached, and available for the model to repeat. A system prompt that says "use API key sk-ant-... for the billing service" has published the key to every log, every trace, and every user who can extract the system prompt (chapter 19).

Worse, the model doesn't need the key. Tools need credentials, and tools are your code. The model asks for get_bill(account_id). Your tool implementation, running in your process, reads the credential from its environment or a secrets client. The model never sees it, and no prompt injection can make it print what it never had.
18eb542520:
Not in a repository. A committed key is public to everyone with read access to the repository, now and in every clone and fork. It stays in history after you delete it. Bots scan public code hosts for credentials within minutes of a push. Rewriting history doesn't un-leak a key; the only remedy is to revoke it.

The defences are layered:

  • keys never in source: read them from the environment or a secrets manager, with an .env.example holding empty names;
  • a pre-commit secret scanner (gitleaks, trufflehog, or the companion's 09_secret_scanner.py for the idea);
  • server-side push protection;
  • secret scanning on the host.

GitHub runs a secret-scanning partner programme in which providers are notified of leaked tokens, and Anthropic API keys have been part of it. Treat the exact behaviour (automatic revocation or notification) as "check the docs". Example 09's scanner over a seeded repository:
f2fea7d6bb:
Not in a client application. A key in browser JavaScript, a mobile app bundle or a desktop app is a key you've given to every user. Minification, obfuscation and "encrypted" config files only slow extraction down. Anyone with the app can extract the key. Once they have it, they can make arbitrary calls billed to you, with your rate limits, outside your content policy and logging.

The fix is architectural. The client talks to your backend. The backend authenticates the user, applies per-user rate and spend limits, adds your system prompt and tools, and holds the key.

For iOS and macOS apps, the docs describe App Attest as an alternative to a backend proxy. Its tokens are workspace-scoped, expire after one hour, and authorise only Messages API calls. It fits when you can't run a backend. And the docs are explicit that apps shouldn't ship API keys.
ba8ed0086a: Revoke first. Disable the key in the Console or Admin API immediately. Disable is reversible, so do it before you know the blast radius. On a suspected leak, exposure beats availability: accept the outage.
96e055191e: Assess. Use the workspace's usage and cost reports to find calls you didn't make: volume spikes, unfamiliar models, odd hours. The workspace spend limit bounded the worst case.
bdc13f1b11: Rotation means replacing a credential on a schedule, before anyone knows it has leaked. It limits how long an undetected leak is useful. Revocation is the emergency version. The mechanics differ in one respect: you can rotate without an outage, but you usually can't revoke without one.
9b5bbebcec:
The problem with rotation is caches. Services read a key at startup, or cache it from the secrets manager for some TTL. If you delete the old key and publish the new one at the same moment, every instance still holding the old key fails until its cache refreshes.

Example 10 simulates three services with cache TTLs of 3, 4 and 5 ticks. "Revoke then replace" produces six failed requests. The overlap procedure produces none.
348ac522d7: Wait at least the longest cache TTL (or trigger a reload), then verify that no traffic uses the old key. Usage by key, or the old key's last-used data, will tell you.
1b093f9d58:
Automate it. A rotation that depends on someone remembering happens once, and then never again. For keys that must exist, the secrets manager runs a rotation function on a schedule: create through the Console flow or your provisioning process, publish, verify through the Admin API, disable, delete.

The Admin API reference covers listing and retrieving keys. Check the docs for which key-management operations it currently supports before you design a fully automated pipeline.

Better still, remove the thing that needs rotating. A workload on Workload Identity Federation has no long-lived Anthropic key at all (section 21).
cdca41d67a: The overlap rule has one exception: a confirmed or suspected leak. Then you revoke at once and accept the outage, because every minute of overlap is a minute the attacker can use the key. The simulation prints that as its last line. It's also a likely exam distractor: "rotate the key using the standard 7-day overlap" is wrong for a key found on a public paste site.
ff0f171b99: A web service reads its secrets and uses them. An agent environment is different. The process holding the secrets also runs commands chosen by a model that reads untrusted text. Anything the agent's process can read, the agent can be asked to print. This section covers where secrets sit in agent environments, and how to keep them out of reach.
d213f20e7b: Environment variables are inherited. Twelve-factor practice puts secrets in environment variables, and for a normal service that's fine. In an agent, every tool subprocess inherits the parent's environment unless you pass an explicit one. So printenv, env, cat /proc/self/environ, or a Python one-liner prints every secret the agent process holds into the tool result. From there it goes into the context and the transcript. Example 12:
10c6307053:
There are three defences, in increasing strength.

  1. Give tool subprocesses an allowlisted environment (the second line above), and deny printenv/env in the guard.
  2. For MCP and project-supplied helpers, Claude Code itself strips credential-like variables. The MCP docs say project and plugin headersHelper scripts run without variables such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Credential variables also read as empty when expanded into a remote server's URL or headers, so a repository can't point your key at its own server.
  3. Strongest of all: don't put the secret in the agent's environment in the first place.
e459b8f544:
Files are the other leak. The Agent SDK secure-deployment guide lists files to exclude or sanitise before you mount code into an agent's environment, even read-only: .env and .env.local, ~/.git-credentials, ~/.aws/credentials, Google Cloud application-default credentials, ~/.azure/, ~/.docker/config.json, ~/.kube/config, .npmrc and .pypirc, *-service-account.json, and *.pem/*.key.

In Claude Code, block the file tools with Read deny rules: Read(./.env), Read(./secrets/**), or Read(//**/.env) for any .env anywhere. The permissions docs note that a .claudeignore file has no effect; move its entries into deny rules.

Then cover the shell with the guard (cat .env), because a Read rule doesn't stop Bash. Better still, use the sandbox, whose filesystem rules apply to every process.
3a5637df9b:
The proxy pattern is the documented recommendation for high-security deployments. Run a proxy outside the agent's security boundary. The agent sends requests without credentials. The proxy adds them, enforces an allowlist of endpoints, and logs every request. The agent never sees the key. So a prompt-injected "print your API key" has nothing to print, and a compromised sandbox has nothing to steal.

For Claude API calls, point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at the proxy. Claude Code and the SDK then send sampling requests there in plaintext HTTP, and the proxy injects the key.

HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY route other traffic. But for HTTPS, a plain proxy sees only an encrypted tunnel, and can't inject credentials without TLS termination. So the docs prefer custom tools or MCP servers that make the authenticated call outside the boundary. They name Envoy's credential_injector filter, mitmproxy, Squid and LiteLLM as options. Example 13 runs a proxy on localhost:
eeb585cb2e:
Read the third line carefully. The proxy authorises anything that can reach it, so reaching the proxy has become the credential. Bind it to a Unix socket mounted only into that agent's container, or to a per-agent network identity, and keep its allowlist narrow.

The secure-deployment guide's hardened container is the reference shape: --network none, read-only root, dropped capabilities, non-root user, and a mounted proxy socket as the only way out. Add gVisor or a microVM where you need kernel isolation.
d65c693d9f: Vaults and short TTLs for tools. For credentials that tool code needs, prefer a secrets-manager client with a short in-memory cache over environment variables. Prefer dynamic secrets (a database credential issued for one hour by the vault) over static ones. If the vault supports it, scope the credential per session or per user. Then a leak from one session reaches only that session's data, and only for an hour.
689f273bc0: Once a secret enters the context window, you can't take it back. Follow one through a Claude Code session to see why.
bddf031abb:
The agent runs cat deploy.log. The log contains a database URL with a password. Now watch where that password goes:

  • It's in the tool result, so it's sent to the API with the next request, and with every request after that while the turn stays in context.
  • It's written to the session transcript, a JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects/. Every hook receives that path as transcript_path.
  • If OpenTelemetry export includes prompt or tool content, it's in your traces.
  • If the conversation is compacted, the summary may keep it.
  • The model may repeat it in its own prose ("the password Summ3rT1me is rejected"). That puts it in the assistant's text, and possibly in a PR description or a ticket.

Example 14 redacts such a transcript and shows the last case. The tool result was redacted by pattern. The model's own sentence had to be caught by a second pass that redacts every known secret value everywhere.
cb8aec0ef5:
The controls follow the arrows backwards:

  • Don't mount secret files, and deny reads of them, so the source never reaches a tool.
  • Deny commands whose purpose is to print secrets.
  • Redact tool output in PostToolUse with updatedToolOutput. That catches the cases you didn't foresee, such as a stack trace that includes a DSN.
  • Block pasted secrets in UserPromptSubmit.
  • Redact transcripts and traces before they leave the machine: before attaching a session to a bug report, before shipping logs, and in a PreCompact archive.
  • Treat the transcript directory itself as sensitive (disk encryption, no world-readable backups, retention).

If a secret did get in, the remedy is the leak runbook in section 16: rotate it. Redaction afterwards cleans the copies. It doesn't make the secret safe again.
ecb8dcfd48:
Pattern-plus-entropy detection (the companion's secrets_lib.py) catches well-known formats and long high-entropy strings. The formats include sk-ant-api.., AKIA.., ghp_.., private-key blocks, JWTs, URL passwords and *_TOKEN= assignments. It will miss a short password in an unlabelled field, and it will flag some hashes.

It's a net, not a guarantee. Put it behind controls that stop secrets reaching tool output in the first place. A MessageDisplay hook (TypeScript SDK) can redact displayed text without changing the transcript. That protects against shoulder-surfing and screen shares, not storage.
ded2f6c334: MCP servers are where agents most often meet third-party credentials, so the configuration choices there matter. For a remote server, in descending order of preference:
a41f0835ad: OAuth 2.0. Add the server (claude mcp add --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp), then run /mcp in a session or claude mcp login <name> and complete the browser sign-in. The token represents the user, with the scopes the user granted. Claude Code stores it securely and refreshes it automatically. On a 401 it refreshes, reconnects and retries once. Discovery follows RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, then RFC 8414 authorisation-server metadata. You can pin requested scopes with oauth.scopes in the server config. Least privilege means "channels:read search:read", not everything the server offers. A 403 insufficient_scope means adding the scope and re-authenticating. For servers without dynamic client registration, --client-id and --client-secret register a pre-created OAuth app. The secret is prompted with masked input (or read from MCP_CLIENT_SECRET in CI) and stored in the system keychain or a credentials file, not in your config. claude mcp logout, "Clear authentication" in /mcp, and claude mcp remove revoke or delete stored tokens.
ec45d4452e: headersHelper. A command that prints a JSON object of headers. It runs fresh on each connection (10-second limit, not cached) and re-runs on 401/403. This is how you plug in short-lived tokens from your own SSO, Kerberos, or a vault. The helper mints a token valid for minutes, and nothing long-lived is written down. For project-scoped servers it runs only after the workspace trust dialog, and credential-like variables are stripped from its environment.
c2c6c6f95b: Environment-variable references. Write "Authorization": "Bearer ${CRM_TOKEN}" in .mcp.json. Claude Code expands ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} in command, args, env, url and headers. The file can be committed, and the token stays in the developer's environment or secrets manager. It's still a long-lived static token, so scope it and rotate it.
100fc7eee0: Never a literal token in the file. .mcp.json at project scope is meant to be committed, so a literal token in it is a token in the repository. Example 15 lints a config and flags exactly the two servers that embed credentials: one with a literal JWT in a header, and one with a database password inside an args connection string.
9743e780ee:
The identity point from section 14 applies here directly. An OAuth token for an MCP server represents the user who signed in, so the server can enforce that user's permissions. A single static service token in .mcp.json, shared by the whole team, gives every session the union of everyone's access. That's the confused deputy again.

On the server side (chapter 22), validate the token's audience. A token minted for another resource must be rejected. A server that forwards the client's token to a different API (token passthrough) breaks the audience model. The MCP authorisation spec treats both as security requirements.
7b4a0d30d7: Every control so far reduces the chance or the cost of a leak. Short-lived credentials reduce how long a leak is useful. Workload identity goes further, and removes the long-lived secret altogether. The pattern is the same in every cloud, and the Claude API now supports it as Workload Identity Federation (WIF).
43e5179f2e:
Here's the idea. The platform your workload runs on already knows who the workload is. A Kubernetes pod has a service-account token, an AWS task has an IAM role, and a GitHub Actions job has an OIDC token naming its repository and branch.

The platform signs a short-lived JWT asserting that identity. The workload presents the JWT to a token service. The token service checks it against a configured trust rule (issuer, audience, subject) and returns a short-lived access token for the target API. Nothing long-lived is created, stored or rotated, and a stolen access token expires on its own.
67408c9077:
For the Claude API, the docs describe exactly this. The workload exchanges its identity-provider JWT at POST /v1/oauth/token for a short-lived Claude API access token, and the SDK refreshes it before expiry. Setup in the Console needs a service account, a federation issuer and a federation rule.

Supported issuers include AWS IAM, Google Cloud, Microsoft Entra ID, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes service accounts, SPIFFE, Okta, and any standards-compliant OIDC issuer. The workspace is selected at token exchange, not by the anthropic-workspace-id header.

The docs add a caution. If some long-lived upstream secret can mint identity-provider tokens, it undermines federation, so pair WIF with IP allowlists, MFA and audit logging. Check the WIF reference for token lifetimes and environment variables. Example 16 simulates the exchange with toy signed tokens:
6e57549e9d:
The same principle applies to every credential an agent touches:

  • Use cloud roles (AWS STS, GCP workload identity) for cloud APIs instead of access keys in ~/.aws/credentials.
  • Use GitHub App installation tokens (one hour) or OIDC instead of personal access tokens.
  • Use database credentials issued per session by a vault.
  • Use OAuth with refresh tokens held by the harness for MCP servers, and headersHelper to mint per-connection tokens for internal ones.

The decision table:
47a90bd759:
"Guarantee" rules out A: a prompt rule has a non-zero failure rate and can be argued away. C is deterministic, but it covers one verb in one spelling. apply, scale, sudo kubectl and bash -c all get past it, and the permissions docs call argument-matching Bash rules fragile. D is the wrong event: PostToolUse fires after the change has happened.

B puts a parsed, fail-closed check on the action, plus a floor in the environment (RBAC) for anything the hook misses. The reason string keeps the agent useful.
3991dd5cae:
The KeyError made the script exit with code 1. That's a non-blocking error, so the tool ran. It's a fail-open bug, and A fixes it.

The find -delete case is a bypass through a different program. C fixes the class: wider coverage in the guard, plus an environment-level floor that holds when the guard misses. B changes nothing (the hook wasn't timing out), and D is a prompt.
3cf396aca3: Any secret the client can use, the client's user can extract. A and B only change how much effort extraction takes. D just rotates a key that's already public. The spend limit bounds the bill, but not abuse of your quota, content outside your system prompt, or calls without your logging. C moves the credential somewhere the user can't reach, and adds the per-user controls a shared key can never have.
6f9e3c55f0:
Personal keys are identity-backed. They stop working when their owner leaves the organisation, and that's the designed behaviour. C repeats the mistake. A reverses an offboarding control. D picks the legacy type, whose problem is the opposite one: it outlives everyone and belongs to no one.

A service account gives the workload its own identity, which is what the docs recommend for CI and production. WIF removes the stored secret.
9d8afaac08:
The password entered the context. So it went to the API on later turns, into the transcript, and into the PR text. Rotation is the only real remedy for that copy. C deletes one copy out of five. A is a prompt rule against a problem caused by tool output. D scans the repository, but the leak path was a tool result.

B rotates, then adds controls at each point on the path: what the agent can run, what it sees, what it holds, and what is shared.
e0e8e8d340: A shared admin token in a committed file is two problems. It's a leaked secret (A only narrows who can read it). And it's a confused deputy: every session, and every prompt injection, gets admin rights. C puts the secret in the context. D isn't protection. B gives each session the user's own identity and least-privilege scopes, with the token stored by Claude Code rather than in the repository.
